items.passage:
可回读的原书范文：

THE IRISH POTATO FAMINE

1. Throughout much of its history, the United States has welcomed immigrants to its shores. People have come because of opportunity, political liberty, and religious freedom. Others have come because of oppression and poverty in their native countries. There is no greater example of the latter reason for immigration than the Irish who fled to this country during the Great Potato Famine of 1845 through 1851. They came because of their failed crops and their resulting starvation, the loss of their homes and possessions to their indifferent landlords, and the ineffectiveness of the English and Irish governments to help them survive.

2. The conditions under which the majority of the eight million Irish lived were shocking. “There never was,” the Duke of Wellington wrote, “a country in which poverty existed to the extent it exists in Ireland.” A census in 1841 reported, “Nearly half of the rural population is living in the lowest state.” People were crammed inside one-room mud cabins without windows or furniture. Farmers slept with their pigs in filthy conditions. Homeless people put roofs over ditches or slept in tunnels they dug in the ground (Woodham-Smith 20).

3. All this misery could be traced to absentee English and wealthy Irish landlords. An 1845 report stated that their property was merely “a source from which to extract as much money as possible.” Landlords leased their land to others who divided it so they could collect more rent. The Irish tenants paid for the right to farm it and to put a cabin up on the property quickly. No money was exchanged, however. The payments were measured by the number of days the tenants worked (Woodham-Smith 20–21).

4. This arrangement depended “entirely and exclusively,” on the potato (Woodham-Smith 35). It grew easily in the bad soil and was easy to cook. The potato was also perfect for feeding pigs, cattle, and chickens. The crop, however, would rot soon after harvesting and could not be stored between growing seasons (Woodham-Smith 35–36). By 1840, one-third of the Irish population depended entirely on the potato for food. It was, “a dependency that teetered on the brink of starvation and created a time bomb that needed only the slightest spark to explode”.

5. That spark exploded in 1845 when the potato crop was attacked by a fungus. The leaseholders dug the potatoes up, only to find that they had turned into “a dark, gooey mess” (The Great Hunger). Six months later, the famine began. It continued and grew worse virtually every year until 1850.

6. At first, the British government tried to help by importing Indian corn from the United States. However, the corn made many people ill, and most tenants had to sell or pawn all their possessions to pay for it. Then the government initiated a second plan: hiring the farm laborers to build roads and canals. By December of 1846, half a million men were breaking rocks up into pieces and shoveling dirt. At this point, however, some workers died of starvation before receiving their wages (Bloy).

7. The famine worsened in 1846 when disease struck the potato crop again. “A stranger,” wrote a sub-inspector of police from County Cork, “would wonder how these wretched beings find food. . . . They sleep in their rags and have pawned their bedding” (Woodham-Smith 92). Unfortunately, much of the food they found was the seed potatoes for next year’s crop. As a result, when the 1847 harvest came in free of disease, it was too small to feed everyone. In 1848, the situation worsened as the blight came back, destroying the entire crop.

8. By this time, even the landlords became desperate. They threw out half a million tenants who could not pay their rent through labor, and then burned their homes. Consequently, many went to live in poor houses. In 1847, however, all public work projects ended, and public poor houses were closed (The Irish Famine). Now with the tenants homeless and living in filth, typhoid fever, cholera, and dysentery broke out, claiming more lives than starvation itself. An official estimate claimed that 750,000 people died from the famine and related causes, but the true number may have been twice as many (Case-Studies).

9. As a result, a million Irish poor fled the country, most of them heading by boat across the Atlantic. The conditions on these “coffin ships” were horrifying, and many people died during the journey. Of those who survived, the great majority went to Quebec and Montreal, Canada, but after arriving, over half walked across the border to the United States. They wanted no part of living in Canada, a British colony (Woodham-Smith 209).

10. The Irish viewed the rapidly growing United States as a land of opportunity. These poor immigrants showed up in rags, without money, education, or skill, but they had a small glimmer of hope. Over the last nearly two centuries, that hope has been fully realized. The Irish population of the United States has more than doubled that of all of Ireland, and an Irish American was even elected to the most powerful position in the United States: John Fitzgerald Kennedy became the first Irish-American president in 1961.

Sources（原书所列）：
1. Bloy, Marjie. The Irish Famine: 1845-9.
2. Case-Studies: Irish potato famine (1845 to 1851).
3. Irish Potato Famine and Trade (History). Web. 10 May 1996.
4. Woodham-Smith, Cecil. The Great Hunger.

词注：absentee = someone who lives a long way away from the property he or she rents to others；teetered = stood or moved in an unsteady way as if going to fall；fungus = a fast-growing mold；pawn = leave something with another in exchange for borrowing money；wretched = unhappy or poor；blight = a plant disease in which parts of the plant dry up and die；cholera = a serious disease of the stomach and bowels caused by infected water or food；dysentery = a serious disease of the bowels that leads to bleeding and passing more waste than normal；glimmer of hope = a small sign of hope。

THE EXPLOSIVE GROWTH OF THE CITIES
By Mark C. Carnes and John A. Garraty

1. By the end of the nineteenth century, immigrants from southern and eastern Europe crowded into cities that were already heavily populated by native-born Americans. As a result, the cities suffered greatly from the effects of rapid growth. Sanitation, fire protection, and the paving of streets were inadequate. Housing was insufficient and overcrowded. Families fell apart, and crime grew out of control. Because of the extent of these problems, however, people eventually took steps to improve living conditions.

2. Sewer and water facilities could not keep pace with the rapidly increasing needs. By the 1890s, the tremendous growth of Chicago had put such a strain on the sanitation system that the Chicago River had become virtually an open sewer. The city’s drinking water contained such a high concentration of germ-killing chemicals that it was almost undrinkable. In the 1880s, all the sewers of Baltimore emptied into the Back River Basin. According to the journalist H. L. Mencken, every summer smelled like “a billion polecats.” Fire protection became less and less adequate. Garbage piled up on the streets faster than workers could carry it away. The streets themselves crumbled beneath the pounding of heavy traffic. Urban growth proceeded with such speed that the cities laid out new streets much more rapidly than they could be paved. Chicago had more than 1,400 miles of dirt streets in 1890.

3. The population explosion also placed a great strain on the housing supply. People poured into the great cities faster than houses and apartments could be built for them. As a result, the densely packed areas of the 1840s became unbearable. Greedy builders used every foot of space, squeezing out light and air in order to jam in a few additional family units.

4. Substandard living quarters aggravated other evils such as the breakdown of family life, along with mental distress, crime, and juvenile delinquency. The bloody New York riots of 1863, for example, were caused in part by the bitterness and frustration of thousands jammed together. A citizens’ committee expressed amazement after visiting the slums “that so much misery, disease, and wretchedness can be huddled together and hidden.”

5. Eventually, however, practical forces operated to bring about improvements. Once the relationship between polluted water and disease was fully understood, everyone saw the need for clean water and decent sewage systems. City dwellers of all classes resented the dirt, noise, and ugliness. In many communities, public-spirited groups formed societies to plant trees, clean up littered areas, and develop recreational facilities. When one city took on improvements, others tended to follow suit, prompted by local pride and competition between cities.

6. Gradually, the basic facilities of urban living were improved. Streets were paved, first with stones and wood blocks, and then with smoother, quieter asphalt. Gaslight, then electric arc lights, and finally Thomas Edison’s incandescent lamps brightened the cities after dark. This illumination of the cities made law enforcement easier. It also stimulated nightlife and permitted factories and shops to operate after sunset. Life in the cities was far from ideal, but streetcars would take people quickly and inexpensively to work and back, and high-rise buildings would soon fill the horizons. The modern American city was forming throughout the East and Midwest.

Source: Adapted from Carnes, Mark C. and John A. Garraty. “American Society in the Industrial Age.”
词注：polecats = skunks—small black and white animals that produce a very strong smell if they are attacked or afraid；aggravated = made a bad situation worse；delinquency = illegal or unacceptable behavior, especially by young people。

missions.instructions: 纠正整篇两段文字中的平行结构错误。原斜体提示为moved、taught、speaking、the Japanese；保留其余原意，可提交完整修订文或逐处“原文→改文”。

items.prompt: Correct the errors in parallelism. Write your correction above the line. The italicized words provide hints as to which structures that follow them may be incorrect.
items.instruction: 完整纠正五处平行形式，不用改写成另一篇文章。
items.answer:
Controversy over immigrants and the language they speak is not new. Millions of Germans moved to the United States in the 1800s and brought their language with them. They not only held their religious services in German, but they also opened private schools in which the teachers taught in German, published German-language newspapers, and spoke German at home, in stores, and in taverns. Eventually all this changed.

The first generation of immigrants spoke German almost exclusively. The second generation assimilated, speaking English at home, but also speaking German when they visited their parents. For the most part, the third generation knew German only as “that language” that their grandparents used. Many other immigrants who came after the Germans have followed the same pattern: the Japanese, the Italians, Eastern Europeans, and many more.
items.explanation: 按答案页逐处核对：①bringing→brought，与moved同为过去时；②speaking→spoke，与taught/published保持过去时；③删去also spoke it，使at home / in stores / in taverns保持介词短语平行；④would speak→speaking，与前面的speaking English并列；⑤删去there are，使many more作为名词性项与各族群并列。原答案印文末尾省去了many more并手写补回；本题依据教材完整句保留many more，只删除there are。

Research immigration trends on the Internet and use your findings to write a summary. Follow the instructions.
1. On an Internet search engine, type in “Immigration from” and add the name of the country in which your parents or ancestors were born. You should find many resources.
2. Select one and find a section that interests you.
3. Then write a one-paragraph summary of the section, beginning by identifying the source, such as “According to Wikipedia, ...” or “James Smith writes in ‘Guatemala: Economic Migrants Replace Political Refugees’ ...”
4. Include a quotation if it is appropriate.

missions.instructions: 以与你、家人或他人有关的历史事件写至少五段因果文章，查阅至少一个来源并引用，同时结合个人知识或经验。完整保留七步写作与原书六项自评；书页231、232两张原评阅表未提供，相关任务单独标缺，不以自编表冒充。

items.prompt: STEP 1: Explore your topic, audience, and purpose.
items.instruction: 确定历史事件、读者和写作目的；写已有知识并查阅一个外部来源，记录新信息。
items.answer: 开放构思：给出事件、读者、说明或娱乐等目的、已有认识、实际来源及新资料笔记。答案册没有统一范文。
items.explanation: 先明确要分析“哪些原因”或“哪些影响”，不要只写历史经过。所选事件也可是一项节日或传统的由来，不一定是政治大事。

items.passage:
Your assignment in this chapter is to write a cause/effect essay about a historical event. Choose a historical event that relates to you, your family, or others—either in another country or in the United States. Write an essay of at least five paragraphs that examines either the causes or the effects of the event. It need not be anything dramatic or political. It could, for example, relate to a festival, a tradition, or a celebration that has a long or interesting history.

Consult one source, either in the library or on the Internet, and use some of the information, including quotations, in your essay.

Develop the body paragraphs with explanations, examples, and even statistics that you find in your research. Do not, however, base your entire essay on what you learn from the source.

Include your personal knowledge of, or experience with, the event, or what you have learned from members of your family. Follow the steps in the writing process.

STEP 1
• Examine what you know, and add to your knowledge about the subject by consulting one outside source. Take notes on what you find.
• Decide on your purpose. Do you want to inform or entertain your readers.

items.prompt: STEP 2: Prewrite to get ideas.
items.instruction: 选择自由写作、头脑风暴或聚类图来探索观点；若画图，用文字的箭头/缩进也可表达关系。
items.answer: 开放构思，无唯一图形。chain应显示各环节先后造成的关系；block应显示并列的原因或影响，旁边补支持材料。
items.explanation: 教材写作提示指出：链式图从上到下连圈，块式图从左到右列圈，支撑材料再向旁边或下面展开。它回指书页15的图，但本页已给出足够操作说明；没有把未提供的15页图伪造成原图。

items.prompt: STEP 3: Organize your ideas.
items.instruction: 写初步论点句，并按chain或block列提纲。
items.answer: 开放提纲，无标准内容。应有一个明确的因果主张，随后各段围绕这一主张展开。

items.prompt: STEP 4: Write the first draft.
items.instruction: 完成至少五段初稿，包含引言、主体和结论；引用一个实际来源，结合自身知识/经验。

In this expansion, you will write a one-paragraph summary of one of the writing models at the beginning of the chapter. Limit yourself to the main ideas of the model, but do not include any of your opinions. Incorporate at least one quotation from the model in your summary. You will have 30 minutes. To complete the expansion, you will need to budget your time accordingly. Follow this procedure.
1. Reread the writing model, underlining the topic sentences of each paragraph. (5 minutes)
2. Write a draft of the paragraph. Be sure to include a title and thesis statement. If possible, combine the ideas of topic sentences, and restate the ideas in your own words. (10 minutes)
3. Revise your paragraph to make sure that a) your ideas are clear and well organized, and b) you have not copied directly from the model. (10 minutes)
4. Check your paragraph for errors. Correct any mistakes. (5 minutes)
5. Hand in your paper to your instructor.

可选原文1：
THE IRISH POTATO FAMINE

1. Throughout much of its history, the United States has welcomed immigrants to its shores. People have come because of opportunity, political liberty, and religious freedom. Others have come because of oppression and poverty in their native countries. There is no greater example of the latter reason for immigration than the Irish who fled to this country during the Great Potato Famine of 1845 through 1851. They came because of their failed crops and their resulting starvation, the loss of their homes and possessions to their indifferent landlords, and the ineffectiveness of the English and Irish governments to help them survive.

2. The conditions under which the majority of the eight million Irish lived were shocking. “There never was,” the Duke of Wellington wrote, “a country in which poverty existed to the extent it exists in Ireland.” A census in 1841 reported, “Nearly half of the rural population is living in the lowest state.” People were crammed inside one-room mud cabins without windows or furniture. Farmers slept with their pigs in filthy conditions. Homeless people put roofs over ditches or slept in tunnels they dug in the ground (Woodham-Smith 20).

3. All this misery could be traced to absentee English and wealthy Irish landlords. An 1845 report stated that their property was merely “a source from which to extract as much money as possible.” Landlords leased their land to others who divided it so they could collect more rent. The Irish tenants paid for the right to farm it and to put a cabin up on the property quickly. No money was exchanged, however. The payments were measured by the number of days the tenants worked (Woodham-Smith 20–21).

4. This arrangement depended “entirely and exclusively,” on the potato (Woodham-Smith 35). It grew easily in the bad soil and was easy to cook. The potato was also perfect for feeding pigs, cattle, and chickens. The crop, however, would rot soon after harvesting and could not be stored between growing seasons (Woodham-Smith 35–36). By 1840, one-third of the Irish population depended entirely on the potato for food. It was, “a dependency that teetered on the brink of starvation and created a time bomb that needed only the slightest spark to explode”.

5. That spark exploded in 1845 when the potato crop was attacked by a fungus. The leaseholders dug the potatoes up, only to find that they had turned into “a dark, gooey mess” (The Great Hunger). Six months later, the famine began. It continued and grew worse virtually every year until 1850.

6. At first, the British government tried to help by importing Indian corn from the United States. However, the corn made many people ill, and most tenants had to sell or pawn all their possessions to pay for it. Then the government initiated a second plan: hiring the farm laborers to build roads and canals. By December of 1846, half a million men were breaking rocks up into pieces and shoveling dirt. At this point, however, some workers died of starvation before receiving their wages (Bloy).

7. The famine worsened in 1846 when disease struck the potato crop again. “A stranger,” wrote a sub-inspector of police from County Cork, “would wonder how these wretched beings find food. . . . They sleep in their rags and have pawned their bedding” (Woodham-Smith 92). Unfortunately, much of the food they found was the seed potatoes for next year’s crop. As a result, when the 1847 harvest came in free of disease, it was too small to feed everyone. In 1848, the situation worsened as the blight came back, destroying the entire crop.

8. By this time, even the landlords became desperate. They threw out half a million tenants who could not pay their rent through labor, and then burned their homes. Consequently, many went to live in poor houses. In 1847, however, all public work projects ended, and public poor houses were closed (The Irish Famine). Now with the tenants homeless and living in filth, typhoid fever, cholera, and dysentery broke out, claiming more lives than starvation itself. An official estimate claimed that 750,000 people died from the famine and related causes, but the true number may have been twice as many (Case-Studies).

9. As a result, a million Irish poor fled the country, most of them heading by boat across the Atlantic. The conditions on these “coffin ships” were horrifying, and many people died during the journey. Of those who survived, the great majority went to Quebec and Montreal, Canada, but after arriving, over half walked across the border to the United States. They wanted no part of living in Canada, a British colony (Woodham-Smith 209).

10. The Irish viewed the rapidly growing United States as a land of opportunity. These poor immigrants showed up in rags, without money, education, or skill, but they had a small glimmer of hope. Over the last nearly two centuries, that hope has been fully realized. The Irish population of the United States has more than doubled that of all of Ireland, and an Irish American was even elected to the most powerful position in the United States: John Fitzgerald Kennedy became the first Irish-American president in 1961.

Sources（原书所列）：
1. Bloy, Marjie. The Irish Famine: 1845-9.
2. Case-Studies: Irish potato famine (1845 to 1851).
3. Irish Potato Famine and Trade (History). Web. 10 May 1996.
4. Woodham-Smith, Cecil. The Great Hunger.

词注：absentee = someone who lives a long way away from the property he or she rents to others；teetered = stood or moved in an unsteady way as if going to fall；fungus = a fast-growing mold；pawn = leave something with another in exchange for borrowing money；wretched = unhappy or poor；blight = a plant disease in which parts of the plant dry up and die；cholera = a serious disease of the stomach and bowels caused by infected water or food；dysentery = a serious disease of the bowels that leads to bleeding and passing more waste than normal；glimmer of hope = a small sign of hope。

可选原文2：
THE EXPLOSIVE GROWTH OF THE CITIES
By Mark C. Carnes and John A. Garraty

1. By the end of the nineteenth century, immigrants from southern and eastern Europe crowded into cities that were already heavily populated by native-born Americans. As a result, the cities suffered greatly from the effects of rapid growth. Sanitation, fire protection, and the paving of streets were inadequate. Housing was insufficient and overcrowded. Families fell apart, and crime grew out of control. Because of the extent of these problems, however, people eventually took steps to improve living conditions.

2. Sewer and water facilities could not keep pace with the rapidly increasing needs. By the 1890s, the tremendous growth of Chicago had put such a strain on the sanitation system that the Chicago River had become virtually an open sewer. The city’s drinking water contained such a high concentration of germ-killing chemicals that it was almost undrinkable. In the 1880s, all the sewers of Baltimore emptied into the Back River Basin. According to the journalist H. L. Mencken, every summer smelled like “a billion polecats.” Fire protection became less and less adequate. Garbage piled up on the streets faster than workers could carry it away. The streets themselves crumbled beneath the pounding of heavy traffic. Urban growth proceeded with such speed that the cities laid out new streets much more rapidly than they could be paved. Chicago had more than 1,400 miles of dirt streets in 1890.

3. The population explosion also placed a great strain on the housing supply. People poured into the great cities faster than houses and apartments could be built for them. As a result, the densely packed areas of the 1840s became unbearable. Greedy builders used every foot of space, squeezing out light and air in order to jam in a few additional family units.

4. Substandard living quarters aggravated other evils such as the breakdown of family life, along with mental distress, crime, and juvenile delinquency. The bloody New York riots of 1863, for example, were caused in part by the bitterness and frustration of thousands jammed together. A citizens’ committee expressed amazement after visiting the slums “that so much misery, disease, and wretchedness can be huddled together and hidden.”

5. Eventually, however, practical forces operated to bring about improvements. Once the relationship between polluted water and disease was fully understood, everyone saw the need for clean water and decent sewage systems. City dwellers of all classes resented the dirt, noise, and ugliness. In many communities, public-spirited groups formed societies to plant trees, clean up littered areas, and develop recreational facilities. When one city took on improvements, others tended to follow suit, prompted by local pride and competition between cities.

6. Gradually, the basic facilities of urban living were improved. Streets were paved, first with stones and wood blocks, and then with smoother, quieter asphalt. Gaslight, then electric arc lights, and finally Thomas Edison’s incandescent lamps brightened the cities after dark. This illumination of the cities made law enforcement easier. It also stimulated nightlife and permitted factories and shops to operate after sunset. Life in the cities was far from ideal, but streetcars would take people quickly and inexpensively to work and back, and high-rise buildings would soon fill the horizons. The modern American city was forming throughout the East and Midwest.

Source: Adapted from Carnes, Mark C. and John A. Garraty. “American Society in the Industrial Age.”
词注：polecats = skunks—small black and white animals that produce a very strong smell if they are attacked or afraid；aggravated = made a bad situation worse；delinquency = illegal or unacceptable behavior, especially by young people。

missions.instructions: 依照原书写一至两段，提出英国政府当时至少一种不同做法，解释它可能如何避免饥荒中的挨饿并产生不同后果。依据已给范文讨论可能性，不把假设写成已发生史实。

items.prompt: Write one or two paragraphs in which you suggest at least one possible action that the English government could have done differently to prevent the Irish from starvation during the Potato Famine. Explain how this action might have resulted in a different effect.
items.instruction: 写1—2段：一项具体替代行动→作用过程→可能产生的不同结果。
items.answer: 开放反事实分析，无官方统一答案。可从范文提到的救济、食物获取、住房或公共工程等问题寻找可改变的行动，但必须具体说明它为什么可能缓解饥饿；不要求某一个政策作为唯一答案。
items.explanation: 不能只写“政府应该做得更好”。把行动和结果之间的中间环节写清，用could have / might have等表达历史假设，避免宣称某方案必然消除所有后果。

Farmers slept with their pigs in filthy conditions. Homeless people put roofs over ditches or slept in tunnels they dug in the ground (Woodham-Smith 20).

3. All this misery could be traced to absentee English and wealthy Irish landlords. An 1845 report stated that their property was merely “a source from which to extract as much money as possible.” Landlords leased their land to others who divided it so they could collect more rent. The Irish tenants paid for the right to farm it and to put a cabin up on the property quickly. No money was exchanged, however. The payments were measured by the number of days the tenants worked (Woodham-Smith 20–21).

4. This arrangement depended “entirely and exclusively,” on the potato (Woodham-Smith 35). It grew easily in the bad soil and was easy to cook. The potato was also perfect for feeding pigs, cattle, and chickens. The crop, however, would rot soon after harvesting and could not be stored between growing seasons (Woodham-Smith 35–36). By 1840, one-third of the Irish population depended entirely on the potato for food. It was, “a dependency that teetered on the brink of starvation and created a time bomb that needed only the slightest spark to explode”.

5. That spark exploded in 1845 when the potato crop was attacked by a fungus. The leaseholders dug the potatoes up, only to find that they had turned into “a dark, gooey mess” (The Great Hunger). Six months later, the famine began. It continued and grew worse virtually every year until 1850.

6. At first, the British government tried to help by importing Indian corn from the United States. However, the corn made many people ill, and most tenants had to sell or pawn all their possessions to pay for it. Then the government initiated a second plan: hiring the farm laborers to build roads and canals. By December of 1846, half a million men were breaking rocks up into pieces and shoveling dirt. At this point, however, some workers died of starvation before receiving their wages (Bloy).

7. The famine worsened in 1846 when disease struck the potato crop again. “A stranger,” wrote a sub-inspector of police from County Cork, “would wonder how these wretched beings find food. . . . They sleep in their rags and have pawned their bedding” (Woodham-Smith 92). Unfortunately, much of the food they found was the seed potatoes for next year’s crop. As a result, when the 1847 harvest came in free of disease, it was too small to feed everyone. In 1848, the situation worsened as the blight came back, destroying the entire crop.

8. By this time, even the landlords became desperate. They threw out half a million tenants who could not pay their rent through labor, and then burned their homes. Consequently, many went to live in poor houses. In 1847, however, all public work projects ended, and public poor houses were closed (The Irish Famine). Now with the tenants homeless and living in filth, typhoid fever, cholera, and dysentery broke out, claiming more lives than starvation itself. An official estimate claimed that 750,000 people died from the famine and related causes, but the true number may have been twice as many (Case-Studies).

9. As a result, a million Irish poor fled the country, most of them heading by boat across the Atlantic. The conditions on these “coffin ships” were horrifying, and many people died during the journey. Of those who survived, the great majority went to Quebec and Montreal, Canada, but after arriving, over half walked across the border to the United States. They wanted no part of living in Canada, a British colony (Woodham-Smith 209).

10. The Irish viewed the rapidly growing United States as a land of opportunity. These poor immigrants showed up in rags, without money, education, or skill, but they had a small glimmer of hope. Over the last nearly two centuries, that hope has been fully realized. The Irish population of the United States has more than doubled that of all of Ireland, and an Irish American was even elected to the most powerful position in the United States: John Fitzgerald Kennedy became the first Irish-American president in 1961.

Sources（原书所列）：
1. Bloy, Marjie. The Irish Famine: 1845-9.
2. Case-Studies: Irish potato famine (1845 to 1851).
3. Irish Potato Famine and Trade (History). Web. 10 May 1996.
4. Woodham-Smith, Cecil. The Great Hunger.

词注：absentee = someone who lives a long way away from the property he or she rents to others；teetered = stood or moved in an unsteady way as if going to fall；fungus = a fast-growing mold；pawn = leave something with another in exchange for borrowing money；wretched = unhappy or poor；blight = a plant disease in which parts of the plant dry up and die；cholera = a serious disease of the stomach and bowels caused by infected water or food；dysentery = a serious disease of the bowels that leads to bleeding and passing more waste than normal；glimmer of hope = a small sign of hope。

rules.title: Cause与effect
rules.explanation: cause回答为什么发生，effect回答导致什么。先确定中心结果或中心原因，再列支撑；不能只按时间先后就断定因果。
rules.example: 原创示例：A lack of sleep may reduce concentration.
rules.before: After the course began, scores rose, so the course must have caused the increase.
rules.after: Scores rose after the course began, but other explanations should also be considered.
steps: 先用一句话写出正在解释的事件：它是你要找原因的“结果”，还是你要分析影响的“原因”。
给每条材料写上“为什么发生”或“发生后带来什么”，把原因和结果放到正确位置。
检查两件事之间的作用过程；若只有先后顺序，补证据或改成可能性表达。

breakdown.note: 范文2先把城市增长过快作为分析起点。
再说明这种增长造成哪些不同生活问题。

breakdown.text: a cause → an explained process → an effect
breakdown.note: 箭头需要理由；“接着发生”本身不能证明“因此发生”。

rules.pitfall: 看到after、then或年份就直接写caused。时间顺序帮助组织叙述，不能独自证明因果。

check.prompt: 原创辅学检测（非教材原题）：开课后分数提高，但没有其他资料。哪一句较严谨？

options.label: The course definitely caused the improvement.
Scores improved after the course began, but other explanations are possible.

check.explanation: b保留观察到的先后关系并承认其他解释；a的definitely比现有证据更强。

rules.sourceLabel: Cause / Effect Essays 书页65（教材PDF第2页）；答案册未提供标准答案/所需附件；书页75（教材PDF第12页）

rules.title: Chain organization
rules.explanation: 一个原因引出结果，这个结果成为下一环原因。适合真正逐环联系的因果链，每一环需解释，而不只是事件列表。
rules.example: 原创示例：Repeated crop failure → food shortage → migration.（结构练习，不额外证明史实）
steps: 列出最初原因、每个中间结果和最终结果，不急着加连接词。
逐环问“这一步怎样促成下一步”，把支持这条联系的解释写在箭头旁。
按这条链安排主体段；引言交代中心事件，结尾说明最终影响。

breakdown.note: 收成减少为什么影响食物供应，要说明依赖该作物等背景。

breakdown.text: food shortage → loss of possessions → migration
breakdown.note: 按范文梳理中间后果时，要解释人们如何被迫卖物、失去居所并迁移；这是一种概括，不表示唯一原因。
原书组织图用这些段落展示逐步展开的后果，最后一段回到移民与融入美国社会。

rules.pitfall: 把几件互不相干的影响串成“所以A、所以B”。没有前后依赖的内容应考虑分块，而不是硬造链条。

check.prompt: 原创辅学检测（非教材原题）：哪组更适合写成chain？

options.label: 停电使冷藏中断，冷藏中断使食物变质。
一种交通政策分别影响费用、噪声和出行时间。

check.explanation: a的前一结果成为后一原因；b列的是并列方面，更适合分别成块分析。

rules.sourceLabel: Cause / Effect Essays 书页72（教材PDF第9页）；答案册未提供标准答案/所需附件

rules.title: Block organization
rules.explanation: 各原因或结果没有直接先后依赖时，按块逐项分析。可以集中多个原因解释一个结果，也可由一个原因分析多个结果。
rules.example: 原创示例：Poor concentration may reflect noise, fatigue, and unclear instructions.
steps: 固定一个中心事件，决定讨论它的多个原因还是多个影响。
把彼此没有直接先后依赖的内容分组，每段只讲一个方面。
每组按“观点—解释—证据”展开，再用合适过渡语连接，结尾回看整体影响。

breakdown.note: 原书城市范文把公共设施问题集中在一段。
住房问题另起一段，不必宣称它由上一段每个问题造成。
继续分方面说明影响。原书图将最后改善部分合写为Paragraph 5，但实际范文改善内容跨第5、6段。

rules.pitfall: 所有段落用then连接，读者会误以为事件逐步发生；列并列方面时用also、another等更合适，但仍须写清关系。

check.prompt: 原创辅学检测（非教材原题）：文章分别分析通勤延长对睡眠、家庭时间和开销的影响，应怎样组织？

options.label: 每个影响各占一段，用证据支撑。
一定写成睡眠减少导致家庭时间减少，再导致开销增加。

check.explanation: 题目给的是三个并列影响，没有证明它们互相造成；按块分别分析更准确。

rules.sourceLabel: Cause / Effect Essays 书页73（教材PDF第10页）；答案册未提供标准答案/所需附件；范文书页68—69（教材PDF第5—6页）

rules.title: 证据与限制语
rules.explanation: 解释机制并用资料、实例、统计或引文支撑；检查遗漏原因、反向因果、过度简化。证据有限时用may/might/contribute to，不把相关性写成必然。
rules.example: 原创示例：Noise may contribute to poor concentration.
steps: 先写段落中的具体主张，再问读者凭什么相信它。
选择能直接支撑该主张的解释、实例、调查、统计或引文，并注明实际来源。
对照证据强度调整用词；无法排除其他因素时使用may、might、possible等，不把复杂现象归为单一原因。

breakdown.note: 这是需要证明的观点，不是写出来就自然成立的事实依据。
原书范文用具体居住环境、数量和当时的引文说明程度。不是每种证据都要凑齐。
原书引入这些限制语，帮助你区分有可能与已确定。

rules.pitfall: 有一个百分比就觉得因果已证实，或者抄了引文却不说明它与观点有什么关系。证据必须相关，因果机制仍须解释。

check.prompt: 原创辅学检测（非教材原题）：只观察到噪声大时注意力较差，哪句强度较合适？

options.label: Noise is the only cause of poor concentration.
Noise may contribute to poor concentration.

check.explanation: may contribute to表示一种可能贡献，没有排除疲劳等其他原因；only超出了这条观察。

rules.sourceLabel: Cause / Effect Essays 书页65（教材PDF第2页）；答案册未提供标准答案/所需附件；书页73—75（教材PDF第10—12页）

rules.title: 因果信号语法
rules.explanation: because/since + 从句；because of/due to/owing to + 名词短语；result in + 结果，result from + 原因；lead to/contribute to 后接名词或动名词。therefore前需句号/分号。
rules.example: 原创示例：The delay resulted from bad weather.
rules.before: The delay resulted in bad weather.
rules.after: The delay resulted from bad weather.
steps: 先把两部分标为原因C和结果E，确定方向后再选连接词。
看连接词后面需要完整句还是名词短语：because + 句子，because of + 名词短语。
通读整句检查方向和标点：result from后是原因，result in后是结果；therefore连接两个完整句时先用句号或分号。

breakdown.text: Because the crop failed, food became scarce.
breakdown.note: 原创拆句示例：because后有主语the crop和谓语failed，是从句。

breakdown.text: Food became scarce because of the crop failure.
breakdown.note: 原创对照：because of后是the crop failure名词短语。

breakdown.text: The shortage resulted from crop failure.
breakdown.note: 原创方向练习：from后为原因；若用in，需要从crop failure写到the shortage。

rules.pitfall: 只翻译中文“因为/所以”，忽略后面是句子还是名词；也不要写两个完整句只用逗号加therefore连接。

check.prompt: 原创辅学检测（非教材原题）：哪一句语法和因果方向都清楚？

options.label: The delay resulted from heavy snow.
The delay happened because of it snowed heavily.

check.explanation: a的from后接名词短语heavy snow，表示原因。b的because of后误接完整句；可改because it snowed heavily。

rules.sourceLabel: Cause / Effect Essays 书页76（教材PDF第13页）；答案册未提供标准答案/所需附件；语法拆句与小检测为原创辅学示例

rules.title: 平行结构与短语动词
rules.explanation: 教材同时训练并列项对称，及put up、depend on、bring about等短语动词的可分/不可分。可分动词带代词宾语时通常把代词置中间。
rules.example: 原创示例：The city needs to improve housing, reduce pollution, and expand transport.
steps: 找and/or连接的各项，标出每项是名词、形容词、动词短语还是完整句。
把同一层级的项调整为相同形式，检查是否可以共用to或其他前置成分。
遇到短语动词，连同具体用法一起确认能否拆开；可分形式带代词时把代词放中间，不及物用法不要硬加宾语。

breakdown.text: to plant trees, clean up littered areas, and develop recreational facilities
breakdown.note: 原书三个动词短语共用to，形成平行结构。

breakdown.text: brought about improvements → brought them about
breakdown.note: 据范文用法改写：bring about可分，代词them放中间。

breakdown.text: depend on the potato → depend on it
breakdown.note: 据范文用法改写：depend on不可拆开；不能写depend it on。

rules.pitfall: 同一个词组在不同用法中可能及物/不及物不同，不能只背词表S/I。原册对turn into、pile up的分类与范文当前不及物句式有不完全对应处，练习中已用自评说明。

check.prompt: 原创辅学检测（非教材原题）：哪句同时保持平行形式和正确代词位置？

options.label: They planned to find the litter, collect it, and throw away it.
They planned to find the litter, collect it, and throw it away.

check.explanation: 三个动词短语共用to；throw away为可分形式，代词it必须放在throw与away之间。

rules.title: 引用与写作流程
rules.explanation: 先找原因/结果和可靠来源，再定chain/block，列提纲、起草、检查论据、修订和校对。引用之后要解释与因果主旨的关系。
rules.example: 原创示例：The report describes a shortage. This shortage may help explain the subsequent migration.
steps: 找一个实际来源，摘录时保留原词和标点，并记录作者、标题或可查位置；先决定这段引文要支撑什么。
把引文嵌入自己的段落：交代来源，按引语位置加标点，再说明它与原因/影响的关系。
按探索、预写、组织、初稿、修订、校对、成稿推进；写完对照任务要求，指定原表缺失时如实标明。

breakdown.text: A census in 1841 reported, “Nearly half of the rural population are living in the lowest state.”
breakdown.note: 原书例句：来源在前，reported后逗号，完整引语首字大写，句号在引号内。

breakdown.text: “The earth belongs to the living,” wrote Thomas Jefferson, “not to the dead.”
breakdown.note: 原书例句：同一句被插入来源说明，后半not保持小写，两侧用逗号隔开。
引用后要说明它支持哪一个意思；整篇文章仍以自己的组织和分析为主。

rules.pitfall: 把改写当逐字引文，或把整段引用扔在段尾不解释。原教材“约四句以上用缩进”的说明是本章示范，实际课程格式要求也要核对。

check.prompt: 原创辅学检测（非教材原题）：哪句正确处理一个被said插开的完整引语句？
check.explanation: 插入语没有结束原引语句，前后用逗号，后半needs不用大写。
